The sound is not very good. This happens when ministers respond in the House.

risks.text: Concerns about high deficits, a lack of transparency regarding the size of the Canadian deficit, and heading toward taxation levels not seen in generations.
Concerns about container shortages over the next six months and labor and capacity shortages in the trucking industry impacting national supply chain resiliency.

unanswered_questions.question: Could the Deputy Prime Minister tell me how much it cost to develop this online AgriStability calculator?
Will the Liberal Party of Canada pay back the money it took from the wage subsidy program, yes or no?
Where is the money toward sexual exploitation and human trafficking?
Will this government condemn that law [national security bill for Hong Kong] today?

summary.text: The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic held its 23rd meeting, during which members presented petitions on various topics such as marine protected areas, Indigenous rights, a no-fault compensation system for vaccine-injured Canadians, streaming royalty models, euthanasia, systemic racism, firearms regulations, and assistance for seniors. Members delivered statements on topics including National Indigenous Peoples Day, front-line health care workers, local celebrations, teachers, and community heroes. During the questioning of ministers, opposition members raised concerns regarding pandemic economic support programs, wage subsidies, commercial rent relief, federal spending transparency, an economic update, foreign policy, forestry sector support, high-speed Internet access in rural areas, and pandemic management. Ministers responded regarding government measures, funding allocations, and ongoing work with provinces and territories.

The meeting of the Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic involved ministerial document tablings, member petitions, and member statements concerning local community efforts, COVID-19 responses, social issues, and international affairs. This was followed by a question period directed at ministers regarding government spending, the Auditor General's budget, the CERB, financial and medical support for sectors such as tourism, agriculture, and energy, personal protective equipment, and various other domestic and international concerns.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session with the Welsh Government, featuring Minister Vaughan Gething, Deputy Minister Julie Morgan, and senior officials. Topics discussed included the impact of COVID-19 on children and young people, health services, critical care capacity, children's mental health and CAMHS services, safeguarding and child protection referrals, looked-after children and foster care, children's rights and impact assessments, and financial support for the childcare sector.

commitments.commitment: Write to the committee regarding a review of unexpected deaths and potential effects of restrictions on children and young people's mental health before the end of the month.
commitments.deadline: before the end of this month

commitments.commitment: Provide a note on funding for third sector services and hospices.
Provide a note on the task and finish group reporting timeline.

risks.text: Parents refusing to engage with the health service and health visitors due to fear and anxiety, potentially leading to a rise in other preventable diseases such as measles.
Potential long-term negative impact on the mental health and emotional well-being of children and young people resulting from lockdown restrictions.
Significant drop in safeguarding referrals to social services during the lockdown period.
Childcare sector providers falling between financial support cracks, with about 50 per cent temporarily closing down due to lack of viable numbers of children.

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held its sixth scrutiny session on the Children (Abolition of Defence of Reasonable Punishment) (Wales) Bill, welcoming witnesses Sally Jenkins (Association of Directors of Social Services), Alastair Birch (Association of Directors of Education Wales), and Councillor Huw David (Welsh Local Government Association). Discussions focused on general support for the Bill, its clarity, implementation, potential impacts on social services and education, awareness-raising campaigns, and resource implications.

decisions.decision: Exclude the public for the remainder of the meeting under Standing Order 17.42.

objections.text: Concern raised that the state should not get involved in family life unless it is in the most serious circumstances.
Concern expressed that anyone accused or convicted of assaulting a child under the new definition will be subject to long-term social services involvement in their family and social stigma.
Concern regarding whether the Bill will divert finances and resources from other areas of children's services and whether local authorities will be properly resourced.

risks.text: Potential double impact on social services in terms of increased referrals due to increased awareness and increased demand for preventative and support services.
Social services departments are overstretched and at breaking point, dealing with children facing serious harm and neglect.

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held a scrutiny session on the 'Healthy Weight: Healthy Wales' draft strategy with Dr Frank Atherton (Chief Medical Officer for Wales) and Nathan Cook (Head of the Healthy and Active Branch at Welsh Government). Discussions covered engagement with children and young people, potential obesity targets, resourcing and the sugar levy consequentials, leadership and governance structures, data and measurement (including the child measurement programme and potential second measurement points), healthy environments and planning rules, school infrastructure and sports facilities, the foundation phase and teacher training/CPD, physical education engagement, free school meals and packed lunches, the review of the clinical obesity pathway, the first 1,000 days, and socioeconomic inequalities.

commitments.commitment: To take back the committee's points regarding foundation phase staffing and curriculum integration to look at how to move from the consultation into the final strategy.

objections.text: Expressed concern that the lack of a target makes it difficult to know if the strategy is achieving its goals or how to properly evaluate it.

Questioned the allocation of sugar levy consequentials in Wales into a general pot to fund a plethora of different things (including vaccination) rather than directly targeting obesity initiatives as done in other UK nations.

risks.text: The consequences of overweight and obesity for young people are going to be enormous if something is not done quite soon, leading to multiple disease issues including diabetes and cancer risk.

unanswered_questions.question: What is the exact Welsh consequential figure from the sugar soft drinks levy?

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session on the Welsh baccalaureate qualification with representatives from ColegauCymru and the Civil Engineering Contractors Association. Participants discussed whether employers and universities understand the Welsh bac, its level of rigor and comparability to other qualifications, student and parental perceptions, and whether it effectively prepares learners for employment.

objections.text: Employers do not have a clear understanding of what the Welsh bac means or includes, and it is not seen as providing the necessary professional skills.
The Welsh bac has turned into a rigorous and demanding qualification that creates heavy burdens in terms of bureaucracy and workload, pushing focus onto outcomes rather than skills.
At foundation and national levels, the Welsh bac involves repetition of what students experienced at school and puts excessive pressure on learners who are already resitting core GCSEs.
Russell Group and other universities outside Wales often do not value the Welsh bac, and admissions tutors may prefer additional A-levels.

risks.text: Prioritizing the Welsh bac and GCSE resits crowds the curriculum and squeezes out other valuable subjects or opportunities, such as modern foreign languages.

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held a scrutiny session focusing on higher and further education with Cabinet Secretary Kirsty Williams, Minister Eluned Morgan, and Huw Morris. Discussions covered teacher training and recruitment (particularly in priority subjects and Welsh-medium teaching), post-16 education and training reforms (including the Hazelkorn recommendations and the PCET Bill), equity and university widening access plans, university mergers, parity of esteem for vocational education and apprenticeships, regional skills partnerships, student mental health and well-being, FE pay disputes, and essay mills.

action_items.action: Publish the summary of technical consultation responses regarding post-compulsory education and training reforms by the end of the week.

Share the review report from the Wales Institute of Social and Economic Research, Data and Methods (WISERD) or similar evaluation documents as discussed regarding regional skills partnerships / Graystone review.
Write to the committee with an update on the timescale and proposals regarding the university student mental health charter and well-being strategic approach.

objections.text: Concern that the cataclysmic drop in people going into teacher training for subjects taught through the medium of Welsh indicates that current answers and levels of ambition do not reflect the required level of action.
Concerns from the further education (FE) sector regarding whether the post-16 reform vision will be truly realised or if the new body will simply be HEFCW by another name.
Concerns regarding the impact of the University of South Wales merger on the Newport campus and the reduction of activity there.

Concern that FE employers are using funding issues as a reason not to provide a reasonable pay settlement and have walked away from the table offering only one per cent, leading to potential industrial action.

risks.text: Risk that Welsh institutions may not have ready access to Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA) data due to changes being made by the Office for Students (OfS) in England.
Financial and operational pressures on FE colleges arising from upcoming pension scheme changes without guaranteed funding from the UK Government.

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session on its inquiry into the impact of Brexit on higher and further education. Kirsty Williams AM (Cabinet Secretary for Education) and Eluned Morgan AM (Minister for Welsh Language and Lifelong Learning), accompanied by officials Huw Morris and Marie Knox, discussed sector preparedness, the potential impact of a 'no deal' Brexit, student recruitment and application trends, funding arrangements including ESF and ERDF, and immigration policies.

risks.text: Exposure and potential impact of leaving the EU in a 'no deal' or 'deal' scenario varies significantly across individual institutions regarding EU student numbers and Horizon 2020 success.
A 'no deal' scenario could lead to a dislocation of companies and a subsequent impact on the number of available apprenticeships.
Potential impact on European Social Fund (ESF) funding and apprenticeships following Brexit.

If third-country status applies under an extended underwrite guarantee for Horizon 2020 and Erasmus, the Welsh HE sector would likely lose about 50 per cent of its current work under those programmes.
A drop in European student applications and the impact of policy changes regarding tuition fee grants for EU students.

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held a session with the Minister for Children and Social Care, Huw Irranca-Davies, alongside Jo-Anne Daniels and Owain Lloyd, focusing on the Welsh Government's childcare offer. Discussions covered early implementer feedback, administrative burdens, rollout plans toward 2020, workforce and capacity challenges (including Welsh-medium provision and children with complex needs), the £4.50 single national hourly rate, additional costs for parents (such as food, snacks, and transport), and comparisons with reports from PPIW regarding work outcomes.

action_items.action: Write to the committee regarding the question about summer-born children and eligibility terms.

objections.text: Concern that the administrative burden on pilot areas and local authorities is too high because parents have to prove eligibility with wage slips and birth certificates.
Concern that the £4.50 single national hourly rate may not be sufficient or appropriate for higher-cost areas like Cardiff, Newport, and Monmouthshire.
Concern that chargeable add-ons (such as food, snacks, transport, and consumables up to £7.50 a day) disproportionately affect lower-income families who cannot afford them.
Concern that the childcare offer policy excludes disadvantaged and workless households, potentially widening the development and school readiness gap.

risks.text: Potential lack of workforce capacity and adequate facilities to deliver the childcare offer across Wales by 2020.
Shortage of Welsh-language childcare provision (meithrin) across parts of Wales.

unanswered_questions.question: How many registered, licensed, and inspected grandparents who look after other people's children are there in constituencies?

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session focusing on targeted funding to improve educational outcomes, specifically examining the pupil development grant (PDG) for free school meals, looked-after children, and adopted children, as well as lessons learned from Schools Challenge Cymru and the role of regional consortia.

action_items.action: Check the exact dates of meetings with Professor Mel Ainscow and report back to the committee
Provide figures for the numbers of staff who transitioned from the Schools Challenge Cymru programme into the consortia

risks.text: The attainment gap for pupils eligible for free school meals widened in 2017 despite PDG levels
Looked-after children have high exclusion rates (over six times more likely to be given a fixed-term exclusion) and their educational attainment results are not good enough

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee met with Estyn representatives (Meilyr Rowlands, Claire Morgan, and Simon Brown) for two evidence sessions. The first session examined targeted funding and the pupil development grant (PDG), discussing targeting towards children eligible for free school meals, support for more able and talented pupils, school leadership capacity, curriculum focus, and services for looked-after and adopted children. The second session scrutinized Estyn's annual report for 2016-17, discussing education reforms, the foundation phase, primary versus secondary school performance, post-16 education, further education colleges, work-based learning, and local authority self-evaluation.

decisions.decision: John Griffiths was appointed temporary Chair for the duration of the meeting in the absence of Lynne Neagle.

action_items.action: Provide a note to the committee detailing specific schools and how much they have closed the attainment gap.
Provide further information and evidence regarding work done with looked-after children and adopted children, including exclusion rates, attendance, and effective practices.

risks.text: Reduction in school budgets causes practical problems for headteachers in having to lay off staff and takes time and energy to deal with cuts.

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session with the Minister for Education Kirsty Williams and Welsh Government officials regarding the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on education in Wales. Key topics discussed included the closure of all schools for statutory education starting the next day, the new operational purpose of schools to support vulnerable children and children of frontline key workers, continuity of free school meals and other support payments (such as EMA and childcare funding), the cancellation of the summer exam series and how grades will be assigned for Year 11 and Year 13 students, and the operational stance of colleges and universities.

decisions.decision: Close all schools in Wales from tomorrow for statutory education provision.
Not proceed with the summer exam series.

action_items.action: Check whether the referral process for additional learning needs outcomes will be suspended or continued as normal.
Look into the ATT qualification and come back to the committee regarding its status.

risks.text: Practical challenges to service delivery at the Student Loans Company due to staff losses from illness, self-isolation, or social distancing.

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session for its inquiry on education otherwise than at school (EOTAS). Witnesses from local authorities, the Welsh Local Government Association, Samaritans, and Mind Cymru discussed the rising number of school exclusions, challenges around additional learning needs (ALN), capacity issues in PRUs and EOTAS provision, teacher training, accountability measures, the impact of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), and mental health support for learners.

risks.text: Rising numbers of school exclusions and lack of system capacity are placing significant pressure on schools and EOTAS provision.
Financial pressures and the implementation of the new ALN Act may place additional strain on schools and local authorities, potentially risking more exclusions.
Delays in accessing EOTAS provision and gaps in education leave vulnerable young people at risk of isolation, negative peer influences, and adverse life trajectories.

unanswered_questions.question: What are the reasons why local authorities experience delays in children accessing EOTAS provision?
What is the impact of home tuition on learners' well-being and how many young people are home-schooled given the lack of central data?

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session on school improvement and raising standards, welcoming Minister for Education Kirsty Williams AM and director of education Steve Davies. The discussion covered the ongoing role of the OECD, implementation and renaming of the national evaluation and improvement resource (formerly toolkit), powers of intervention in schools causing concern, regional consortia and local government roles, performance measures, PISA targets, and closing the attainment gap for disadvantaged and minority groups.

decisions.decision: Change the name of the 'national evaluation and improvement toolkit' to the 'national evaluation and improvement resource'.

commitments.commitment: Publish the latest OECD report on Welsh education on 23 March and make a statement to the Chamber on 24 March.
Introduce the national evaluation and improvement resource across the system at the start of the new academic year in September 2020.

action_items.action: Write to Neath Port Talbot to ask them to demonstrate how they are going to meet their functions if they pull out of ERW.
Send a note regarding when the permanent performance measures and qualifications review is expected to be completed.

objections.text: Neath Port Talbot gave notice that they want to withdraw from regional working (ERW).

risks.text: Secondary schools present a particular challenge and the same schools are persistently identified as needing the highest level of support without moving at pace away from that system.
New headteachers taking over a school represent a moment of risk in school leadership changes.

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held a scrutiny session on early childhood education and care with Deputy Minister Julie Morgan and Welsh Government officials Jo-anne Daniels and Nicola Edwards. Discussions focused on the dual objectives of supporting child development and helping parents into work, the complexity and simplification of the early years system, local authority pathfinder projects, the childcare offer, Welsh language provision, and Flying Start targeting.

commitments.commitment: Send through the last term's data on children accessing the childcare offer in Welsh only.
Share more detail on comparative costings for the childcare system once worked up.

objections.text: Concern that cuts to the education improvement grant and fewer teaching assistants in the system will impact standards in the foundation phase.
Frustration regarding the money and time spent on the HMRC childcare funding route before it was suspended.

risks.text: Recruitment and retention within the childcare and play sector is challenging, and recruiting and retaining staff with good Welsh language skills adds an extra dimension of difficulty.

unanswered_questions.question: How much money has the Welsh Government secured for early years from the most recent UK Government announcement?

summary.text: The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session to scrutinise the Welsh Government's progress in developing the new curriculum for Wales. Minister for Education Kirsty Williams AM, along with officials Steve Davies and Claire Bennett, discussed feedback from the draft curriculum engagement period, plans for refining the guidance, changes to the primary legislation (including statutory provisions for 'what matters' statements and progression frameworks), feedback on religious education and relationships and sexuality education, professional learning investments, accountability frameworks, and implementation timelines targeting September 2022.

decisions.decision: To publish the final version of the curriculum in January 2020.
To introduce the Education Bill following the Easter recess.
To include statutory provisions for the 'what matters' statements within the legislation.
To include in the legislation provision for a statutory framework setting out the approach to progression in each area of learning and experience (AoLE).

action_items.action: Provide the committee with a list of the new innovation schools.

objections.text: Concerns and objections regarding the inclusion of a range of faiths and world religions in religious education (RE), with many calling for a clearer and stronger focus on Christianity.
Objections to religious education and relationships and sexuality education (RSE) being compulsory parts of the curriculum, with views that RSE should be solely the preserve of parents.

risks.text: Concern that the new curriculum could exacerbate segregation within schools between different groups of pupils.

Concerns from classroom teachers that there will be a different accountability framework to the aims and objectives of the new curriculum and that there will be no consistency across schools in how it is delivered.

summary.text: The project team met to discuss the functional design of the new TV remote control, incorporating three new company requirements: excluding teletext, restricting functionality solely to controlling the television, and including corporate colors and the slogan. Presentations were delivered by the User Interface Designer, Marketing, and the Industrial Designer. The team decided to target the 15-35 age demographic, include basic remote functions (on/off, volume up/down, channel up/down, channel numbers, and mute) with advanced features potentially hidden or grouped, stick to regular batteries instead of a rechargeable docking unit, rely on traditional infra-red transmission, and organize controls into three conceptual buckets (audio, video, and device).

decisions.decision: Exclude teletext functionality from the remote control.
Restrict the remote control to control only the television.
Incorporate the corporate color and slogan into the new design.
Target the 15 to 35 age bracket.
Stay with traditional infra-red transmission.
Use regular batteries rather than a rechargeable charging unit.
Organize controls into three buckets: audio, video, and device.

objections.text: Speech recognition technology may not be simple enough for users and could be expensive or unreliable.

risks.text: If the project becomes too complex, it will affect the time to market.
Using infra-red transmission can cause line-of-sight blockage issues if someone stands in front of the receiver.

unanswered_questions.question: Whether the corporate slogan should be actually written on the remote control or just embodied as an idea.
What the exact retail price of the remote control will be.

summary.text: The meeting is the final detailed design and evaluation meeting for the remote control project. The team reviews the prototype and discusses specifications, including the size (approximately ten centimetres in height, three and a half centimetres in width, and two point five centimetres in depth), the removal of the LCD screen and advanced chip due to cost constraints, relying instead on the TV screen to display functions via a regular chip, and using a jog-dial for volume and advanced functions. They confirm the remote will use a battery and a double-curved plastic case. Finally, they review the design evaluation criteria, discuss their satisfaction with the project's creativity, leadership, teamwork, and tools, and conclude the meeting.

decisions.decision: Use a battery for power due to cost restraints instead of kinetic power.
Use a double-curved plastic case.
Remove the LCD display panel and the advanced chip to save costs, replacing the advanced chip with a regular chip and using the TV screen to display functions.
Use normal-coloured buttons to cut costs.

objections.text: Concern raised about using yellow because it is the company's colour and may not be a hit with customers.
Concerns regarding the constraints of the meeting structure, guidelines, and equipment (such as wearing recording glasses) which restrict creativity and teamwork.

risks.text: The project was initially over budget, requiring features like the LCD screen and advanced chip to be removed.

summary.text: The project team met to evaluate the prototype for their new remote control, discuss budget constraints, review marketing criteria, and agree on product specifications such as retaining the LCD display, using a plastic solid case, single-curved design, and a special yellow color. They also evaluated team performance and project satisfaction.

decisions.decision: Keep the LCD display despite the cost it incurs.
Go with a plastic solid case to keep within budget.
Adopt a single-curved design that still allows articulation.
Use a special yellow color for the case.

objections.text: The industrial designer raised concerns that the plastic casing would not be as comfortable on the hand.
The marketing representative noted that the prototype product will score very badly on some of the evaluation criteria because certain features were totally abandoned.
Participants noted that a remote control with only two buttons and a joystick might be daunting and confusing for technophobic or older users.

risks.text: The project was four Euros over budget, forcing compromises such as ditching the USB connection and potentially dropping the locator feature.
Transmitters, receivers, and speakers were initially not factored into the cost estimates.

unanswered_questions.question: Whether a point five Euro cost for a push button applies per button or generally, and whether the joystick/scroll wheel pricing is correct.

summary.text: The team held their second meeting to discuss the design and requirements of a new remote control. They reviewed findings from market research, discussed physical features such as a flip-open/sea-shell design, rechargeable docking station, and touch/button layout, and noted new project requirements including limiting the control to TV only (and video), omitting teletext, incorporating corporate image/logo, and avoiding speech recognition due to cost. They also discussed ways to locate lost remotes via a base station beeper and addressed customer service and instruction manuals.

decisions.decision: The control will be for TV only.
Teletext will not be used.
The remote will use rechargeable batteries with a docking station.

objections.text: Speech recognition would likely be too expensive to incorporate.
Concerns regarding how to address repetitive strain injury (RSI) with small screens or movements.

risks.text: Remotes are small and easily lost down the back of the sofa.

summary.text: The team held a conceptual design meeting to discuss remote control properties, materials, user-interface options, and market trends. They decided on using kinetic charging with watch-type batteries, a flip-top design with an LCD display on the top side, rubberised anti-RSI buttons on the bottom side, a plastic case housing with a rubberized sleeve cover available in fruit and vegetable colors, and discussed investigating voice recognition or a whistle feature for locating the remote.

decisions.decision: Use kinetic charging
Use watch-type batteries
Use an LCD display on the top side of the flip-top
Use rubberised buttons on the bottom side
Use a plastic case housing
Use a rubberized sleeve cover for the case
Use fruit and vegetable colors for the rubber cover

risks.text: Voice recognition feature might be too expensive

unanswered_questions.question: Will voice recognition be financially feasible to incorporate?

summary.text: The team reviewed prototype designs and evaluated the product against market research criteria. They agreed on design features such as a plastic body with a changeable rubber outer casing, kinetic batteries, standard transmission chips, infrared placement at the front, and dual screens (an inset black-and-white touch screen on top and standard buttons on the bottom). After rating criteria like fancy look and feel, technological innovation, ease of use, fashion trends, RSI minimization, and ease of location, they concluded that the product meets specifications well enough to proceed. They discussed the budget, deciding to remove the voice recognition feature to fit within the financial target.

decisions.decision: Use a kinetic charger/battery.
Use a standard chip.
Include a stand-by function.
Make the case material soft, rubbery, and changeable.
Use buttons with a combination of LCD and rubber.
Use bright funky designs inspired by fruit.
Use anti-RSI rubber buttons.
Remove the voice recognition system from the standard product to meet the budget.

risks.text: The repetitive strain injury (RSI) minimization criterion received lower neutral ratings compared to other criteria.

summary.text: The team met to review marketing potential and user interface/industrial design concepts for a new television remote control. They discussed constraints from management such as the removal of teletext, keeping the design for a specific television, and incorporating corporate yellow colors and the slogan 'put the fashion in electronics'. The team voted and decided on key features for the remote control, including speech recognition, a limited number of buttons, an organic design, programmability, and a glow-in-the-dark trim.

decisions.decision: Drop teletext from the remote control design.
Incorporate corporate colour yellow and the slogan 'put the fashion in electronics' into the remote control design.
Use speech recognition for the remote control.
Limit the number of buttons on the remote control.
Adopt an organic design for the remote control.
Include button programmability options.
Include glow-in-the-dark material trimming as a gimmick.

action_items.action: Find out what people think about removing teletext or whether people require a teletext option in a remote control.
Put all reports in the project documents folder.

objections.text: Speech recognition can suffer from noise interference problems (such as picking up TV audio or advertisements and changing channels unintentionally).
TFT screens are fragile, expensive, and likely to break or get damaged since remotes get abused and thrown around.

risks.text: Glow-in-the-dark material needs light to charge and will not glow if left sitting in the dark for too long or under couch cushions.

summary.text: The team discusses findings from market and user surveys regarding the remote control design, focusing on fancy outlooks, technological innovation (including speech recognition), ease of use, material feel, color choices, and power sources. They also agree to work on a clay model of the remote control for the next meeting.

decisions.decision: Incorporate speech recognition software into the remote control design.
Use a rechargeable battery system.

action_items.action: Work on giving a model in clay for the next meeting.

risks.text: LCD technology might be too expensive for the budget and confusing for ease of use.

summary.text: The project manager introduced the design project to create an original, trendy, and user-friendly TV remote control with a production cost maximum of twelve and a half Euros to reach a profit target of fifty million Euros. Team members introduced themselves and shared their roles: Cat as Marketing Expert, Maarika as Interface Designer, Gaurav as Industrial Designer, and Jen as Project Manager. The team discussed preliminary design ideas, such as a buttonless design or menu-based interface, and noted that they will continue working individually on their respective design components before the next meeting.

unanswered_questions.question: Whether there is any special feature that we want to have this remote control have as opposed to the already existing ones?

summary.text: The team held their final detailed design meeting for the remote control project. They presented the prototype (shaped like a banana with a rubber casing, LCD screen, and voice recognition), evaluated the design against their criteria (achieving an average score of about 6.5), reviewed production costs using an Excel spreadsheet to ensure the product was within the 12.5 budget, and provided feedback on the overall project and design process.

decisions.decision: Use the approximate shape and color of a banana for the remote control design.
Make the remote control case out of rubber.
Put a locator dot on the TV to make the remote locatable with a beeping sound.
Remove the sample sensor from the design to cut production costs and stay within the budget.
Remove the scroll wheel and replace it with push buttons on the side to stay within the budget.

action_items.action: Put the evaluation scores in the project documents file.
Complete the final questionnaire and meeting summary when they are sent.

risks.text: The current design is more suitable for right-handed people than left-handed people.

summary.text: The team held an initial meeting for a new remote control project, covering tool training via whiteboard drawings, project financial and production constraints (including a 25 Euro selling price and 12.50 Euro production cost ceiling), and brainstorming sessions on remote control designs, ultimately leaning toward a reliable television remote with ergonomic and practical features.

objections.text: Expressing concern that a multi-device or multi-sided remote control design would be too complicated, expensive, or difficult to use.

risks.text: Making something that controls everything might be too expensive to produce within the 12.50 Euro unit cost limit.

summary.text: The project manager and team members (Catherine for Industrial Design, Gabriel for User Interface, and Reissa for Marketing) held a meeting to present their initial work on designing a television remote control. Each member gave a brief presentation covering working design, user interface research, and marketing findings. The team decided to go with a basic television remote utilizing infrared signals and standard batteries, and discussed corporate design image and ergonomics.

decisions.decision: Use infrared signal for the remote control transmission.
Use batteries as the energy source for the remote control.
Scrap voice activation for the remote control.

action_items.action: E-mail e-mail addresses to the project manager

summary.text: The team held a detailed design meeting to review three remote control prototypes (rhombus, potato/mango, and Martian), evaluate the chosen 'potato/mango' shape against various design criteria, verify financial costs against the budget, and conduct a project process evaluation.

decisions.decision: Choose the potato (or mango) shape for the remote control prototype.
Do not worry about the remote losing feature for now and rely on bright designs to stand out.
Add an extra button on the top for on/off.
Include an 'RR' corporate logo on the remote control.
Keep the remote control case material as rubber.
Use six buttons on the remote interface.

Concern that the digital pen was a bit distracting due to its heaviness and being conscious of turning pages.

summary.text: The team held a conceptual design meeting for a new remote control. They reviewed presentations on trend watching, interface concepts, and component design, and made several decisions regarding the remote's energy source, materials, and features.

decisions.decision: Decided against using a charging base with rechargeable batteries for the remote.
Decided to use batteries (instead of a charging base).
Decided to incorporate a finding/locating device in the remote.

Decided to use yellow for the button illumination color.

action_items.action: Work together on a prototype using modeling clay.

Expressed concern that key finders activated by whistling become highly irritating when triggered accidentally.
Expressed concern that putting a company logo on a button is a bad idea because buttons wear off.

unanswered_questions.question: What size batteries (double-A or triple-A) should be used?
